## Issue 02 — Halyard (pages 19–36)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 19.** "They saw it." / "Seeing isn't the same as changing." Good opener. It picks up right where Issue 1 left off.
- **Page 21, panel 1.** 312 patents. Wait, the gambler dad was an *inventor*? That's a real twist and I wanted to know more.
- **Page 21, panel 4.** "Protected from what?" / "From being asked to choose while frightened." Lock is creepy-polite, and I liked hating him. Best villain line in the book.
- **Page 22, panel 4.** "You can still walk away." / "That's what he's selling." Good.
- **Page 25.** Jalen: "I'm not coming with you." / "You already are." / "That's not reassuring." The only collaborator with a personality.
- **Page 27–28.** The build fails at 11%. Then Alex feels the edges: "The parts aren't wrong. The edges are." This ties back to page 1, where he fixes things by touch. I liked seeing his one skill matter. "I expected a longer failure." / "You can have one later." Funny.
- **Page 30, panel 4.** "I counted the record and missed the people. That was my error. What would you do?" The robot admitting it was wrong was the most interesting character beat in this issue.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 20.** This is where I checked out. A kiosk that takes a girl's invention and gives her 14 credits, then a "fair price" purifier shop with its wage and margin on a screen. Then the robot explains, "One business earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale." It's an economics worksheet with pictures. I skimmed the whole page and rolled my eyes.
- **Pages 23–26.** Collect four parts from four people, one page each. It felt like a video game fetch quest. Each person hands over a thing, says one wise sentence and a door closes. By Ren I was skimming.
- **Pages 31–32.** I thought they'd already won on page 28 (94%), so building it all again two pages later dragged.
- **Page 33.** "PATENT STATUS: UNFILED" / "No exclusive owner." Message received. It felt like the moral being handed to me.

### I was confused
- **Page 22, panel 3.** "Including Lina. Suri. Jalen. Ren." Who are these people? I'd never heard of any of them, and Alex rattles off four names like he grew up with them. How does he know them? This is the moment I felt most locked out of the book.
- **Page 22, panel 1.** "Caldera can build the purifier faster." *What* purifier? First mention.
- **Page 21.** "Charter Compact." What's that? Never explained.
- **Page 21–22.** If his dad had 312 patents, why is the family drowning in debt? Nobody says.
- **Page 23.** "This is not the Keel routing failure." So there are two water problems now? I thought the problem was stolen water. Now it's dirty water too, and a purifier fixes the dirty part but not the stolen part? I had to stop and sort this out.
- **Page 25, panel 4.** "Five people. Two machines. The patrol will classify six active bodies." Which five people? Five plus two is seven, so the joke is that TJ doesn't count? I read it three times.
- **Pages 26–27.** Doors close between the group and Ren and the others. Then one page later all of them are in a maker room together. How did they get there?
- **Page 28 vs pages 32–33.** 94%, then cloudy water, then 91%. Is cloudy water good? Was the first one fake? I lost the thread of what "winning" meant.
- **Page 34.** He refuses, and Lock says the Houses will decide anyway. Then page 36 says "HOUSE PRODUCTION AUTHORIZED." So what did refusing get him? Do the collaborators still lose their jobs? Page 36 says "ACCESS REVIEW PENDING," so maybe yes? I couldn't tell if this was a win.
- **Page 35.** Where did the medallion come from? What does it *do*? It warms up and the screen says "CONTRIBUTION ATTRIBUTION REGISTERED." So the magic dad artifact is a… copyright form? That was a letdown.
- **Page 36.** "Covenant band," "ESCALATION: UNAVAILABLE UNDER STANDING SCOPE," "BOUNDED SUMMONS ISSUED." I didn't understand any of this. *Confused and detached.*
- **Where is Tomas?** Issue 1 ended on "SIGNAL LOST," and nobody in Issue 2 mentions him once. Alex doesn't ask. That bugged me more than anything else in this issue. The one character I cared about got dropped.
- **Where did Ada and TJ go?** Ada gets about three lines. TJ fetches a fastener.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Caldera / Vector / Orbital House | p19 | Barely. Big companies, I think. I couldn't tell them apart. |
| "The Houses" | p20 | Big companies, chosen "by Alpha." Still no Alpha explanation. |
| Morrow & Sons | p20 | A nice small shop. It comes back on p54. |
| Charter Compact | p21 | Never. |
| Director Cassian Lock | p21 | The name, and that he's the bad guy. Not what he's director *of*. |
| Lina, Suri, Jalen, Ren | p22 (named) / p23–26 (met) | Met them after Alex already knew them. |
| The purifier | p22 | Built on p32. |
| The Measure | p23 (named) | Okay. Now I know the p14 thing has a name. |
| Maker's Seal | p35 | It "registers attribution." That's all I ever learn. |
| Covenant band | p36 | Explained on p41. |
| "Scope," "bounded," "standing" | p36 | Never, really. |

### Lines I read twice
- p20: "One business earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale."
- p21: "Rights under dispute are not a wallet."
- p21: "From being asked to choose while frightened." (Read it twice because it was good.)
- p23: "The Measure showed where water went. This is what's in a different feeder."
- p23: "My access is already being counted."
- p25: "Five people. Two machines. The patrol will classify six active bodies."
- p26: "Waste heat is still material. Vent it and you lose the system."
- p27: "Not when nothing is allowed to share."
- p29: "I said protection was available."
- p35: "I carried it until someone proved they understood what it was for."
- p36: "ESCALATION: UNAVAILABLE UNDER STANDING SCOPE." Gave up.

Something I noticed by this issue: **everyone talks the same way.** It's always a short two-part fortune cookie, X isn't Y: "Seeing isn't the same as changing." "Time is useful. It isn't a replacement pipe." "Thinking about it isn't doing it." Ada, Lina, Suri, B11 and Lock all do it. That's the moment I started wondering if a person wrote this, and people in my class would say it out loud.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- **Clear:** Alex, B11, Lock, Jalen.
- **Blurred:** Lina, Suri and Ren. I knew them by their part (membrane, living filter, heat), not by personality. If you swapped their lines I wouldn't notice. Suri is a little prickly. That's it.
- **Faded out:** Ada and TJ.
- **Faceless:** the three House representatives.

### I felt something
- p10–p30 bridge: B11 saying "That was my error. What would you do?" A little moment.
- p28: the fix landing. A small *nice*.
- Not much else. I didn't care about the four collaborators losing their jobs because I'd known each of them for one page.

### I predicted
- From p21: he won't sign. (Correct, and obvious.)
- From p29: they'll build it without patents and share it. (Correct.)
- From p36: Mera is going to turn out to be connected to the dad.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Alex has to decide whether to sell his dad's inventions to a big company to clear his debt, or share them with the people who actually made them.

That's a different book from the one I thought I was reading after Issue 1, which was about stolen water and a missing dad. Neither of those comes up much in this issue.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 20.** The kiosk and the fair-price shop page with the robot explaining it was the shelf moment. Page 22's list of four strangers would have finished it.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
No. A woman I don't know pushes a button called SUMMON on a screen full of words I don't understand. Nobody I care about is in danger. The cliffhanger is a menu. The only reason I'd open Issue 3 is that it's called "Oasis" and I still want to know what happened to the dad. The book has made me wait 36 pages for that.

VERDICT Issue 02: put down: page 20; next issue: no

---

## Issue 03 — Oasis (pages 37–54)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 37, panel 2.** "VEYRA, A. — RESIDENT RECORD FOUND." / "It knew my name." Ada is *from* the rich city? Real surprise. I sat up.
- **Pages 38–40.** The Ada and Leona scene is the best writing in the book. "I stopped asking whether that meant dead or unwilling." "Within a year." / "And you didn't come." "You chose safety instead of me." These are real people saying real, painful things, and for the first time nobody was teaching me anything. I liked that Alex stays in the hallway.
- **Page 40, panels 3–4.** Mera walks in: "I promised Leona I would keep you safe." / "You watched me." / "I did." / "Watching is not knowing." / "Then don't call it care." This went back and changed page 8 for me: she was watching *Ada*. Cool.
- **Page 44.** "First, people stopped selling to him. Then people stopped standing near him." That was chilling, and the only time Alpha felt scary instead of like paperwork.
- **Page 45.** The flashback, with water under the door and the dad sending the robot away. "Alex. What you do with this is up to you." It hit.
- **Page 46.** "He left me the debt. The silence. The machine." / "He left you a choice." Then "He was still a gambler." / "Yes." / "And he still built something worth finding." / "Also yes." Good, and B11's "Also yes" made me smile.
- **Page 52.** Tomas is ALIVE. Then "Paper says sixty-two." / "Pipe says eighteen." This was the best callback in the book. It turns the Issue 1 reveal into a weapon, and the guy who saved Alex is the one holding it.
- **Page 53.** "The allocation is compliant." / "The water isn't." Good line.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Pages 41–42.** The bands, which one is which metal, two of three custodians, the deciding vote. I had to slow down to get it, then it turned into a recorded confession at a terminal.
- **Page 47.** "THREE COMPONENTS DETECTED / HUMAN ROLE REQUIRED: CONVENOR / AUTHENTICATOR." Skimmed.
- **Pages 49–51.** I skimmed almost all of these: "DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL," "EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED WITHIN DEFINED SCOPE," "ALPHA ROLE: OPERATION / MONITORING / MAINTENANCE / ACCOUNTING / ALERTS," "EXISTING DEBT, OWNERSHIP, ALLOCATIONS AND AGREEMENTS: UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS." The climax of the book is three nameless people saying one phrase each, then all-caps screens. It's a civics test.

### I was confused
- **Page 41.** "We built the Covenant during the Water War." So *this* is what everything has been about? A Water War, an emergency, three custodians, and Adrian was one of them? The gambler dad from the casino was one of three people who handed the world to an AI? That should be the biggest reveal in the book, and it's one panel on page 41. Everything I needed in Issue 1 shows up here.
- **Page 41.** Why does B11 have Adrian's band in his chest? It was never shown before.
- **Page 42.** The bands "link and glow." What does that do?
- **Pages 45–46.** Is Adrian dead? The flashback cuts away. Grandma said on page 4, "He's closer than you think." That's never explained. Is he alive somewhere? Was she just confused? I wanted that answered more than anything else, and the book acts like it was never asked.
- **Page 47.** Mera's dark band "remains apart" on page 42, then gets put on the node on page 47. Did she agree? When?
- **Page 48.** She offers him total power and he almost takes it. It isn't clear why she has the right to offer it, if her own override failed on page 44.
- **Page 48, panel 4.** "Don't give me that much power." Is Ada saying she doesn't trust herself? Or him? I read it twice.
- **Page 50.** Who are these three people? They decide the fate of the world, and I don't know their names.
- **Pages 52–53.** Where is Tomas? He's in Keel checking a gauge, but the vote is in Oasis. Is he on a screen? Then he's talking in the hall? I couldn't place him.
- **Page 52.** So the water was *still* at 18% weeks later? What happened to the miners opening the valve on page 17?
- **Page 54.** His debt went from 418,607 to 402,110. That's 16,000 credits paid off in "weeks" when he makes 40 a day and just lost his workshop. Math kids will catch it. I did.
- **Page 54.** Where are B11 and TJ? The robot is basically the reason I kept reading, and he's not on the last page.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Leona Veyra | p38 | Yes, Ada's mom. Clear. |
| Covenant | p36 / p41 | Yes, on p41. |
| The Water War | **p41** | One line. That's all. |
| Alpha's emergency authority | p41 | Yes, finally, on page 41 of 54. |
| Three custodians | p41 | Yes. |
| Convenor / authenticator | p47 | No. |
| Distributed Verification Protocol | p50 | No. It's a screen title. |
| "Within defined scope" | p51 | No. |
| The water-drop mark (from Issue 1) | p4 | Never explained. |
| The casino chip equation (from Issue 1) | p2 | Never explained. It just gets set down on p46. |

### Lines I read twice
- p40: "I traded a few terrible days I could see for fifteen years I couldn't." (Worth it once I got it.)
- p41: "Alpha recorded 'later' as permission to continue." (Same, a good line.)
- p42: "I will support a process where affected people can see what is promised and call it broken." Gave up halfway.
- p44: "I gave it authority to move faster than I could stop."
- p47: "I convene it. I don't own it."
- p48: "Don't give me that much power."
- p50: "The proposal is public. The obligation is public. The people affected can challenge it."
- p51: every screen on the page.
- p54: "You still thinking about leaving?" / "Every day." / "Good." Why is that good? I think she means he still has the choice. I wasn't sure.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- **Clear:** Ada (finally a full person), Leona, Mera (finally a person, on page 40), Alex, B11, Tomas.
- **Couldn't:** the Keel gauge worker, the Halyard representative, the Oasis clerk and the House representative. They're job titles. The ending belongs to people I can't name.
- **Gone:** Lina, Suri, Jalen and Ren. They built the purifier, then disappear. I don't know whether they lost their jobs.

### I felt something
- p39, "You chose safety instead of me." This was the biggest one.
- p45, the dad in the flooding room, saying his son's name.
- p46, "Also yes."
- p52, Tomas alive. Relief, then a grin at "Pipe says eighteen."
- p54, mixed. I respected that he's still in debt and nothing is magically fixed. I also felt cheated. He did all that, lost the workshop and his travel pass, and paid down about 4%. Some of my class will call this "realistic." Most will call it "so what was the point."

### I predicted
- From p37: Ada's family is powerful. (Sort of right.)
- From p43: the dad is alive in the station. (Wrong. He's gone, maybe dead, the book won't say.)
- From p48: he won't take the power. (Correct, and obvious from the moment it was offered.)

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid refuses to become the new ruler after finding out his dad helped hand the world to an AI, and instead sets up a slow public process where people can challenge the system.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 51.** Two pages of all-caps screen language at the climax. Pages 38–46 had me, then it turned into a council meeting. Tomas on page 52 pulled me back, but in a shop I'd already have closed it.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
For the book overall: no. The last page is quiet, two people looking over a half-dry basin. It ends a book; it doesn't ask for another. I got some of what I wanted (the water, Tomas, Ada's mom). The thing I wanted most, what happened to the dad and what Grandma meant, got left on the table, and that isn't a hook because the book doesn't seem to know it's open. I wouldn't buy a sequel.

VERDICT Issue 03: put down: page 51; next issue: no

---

## The whole book

### The page that would have lost my whole class
**Issue 02, page 20.** The contribution kiosk, the "fair price" shop with its wage and margin on the screen, and the robot explaining that the Houses "were selected for scale." Everyone would recognize this as the econ lesson the book was assigned for. After that, nobody believes the story isn't a worksheet. The ones who survive it get lost two pages later on "Lina. Suri. Jalen. Ren." Anyone still reading in Issue 3 gets lost on page 51.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
"A kid gets stuck with his dead-beat dad's debt, finds a really funny robot his dad left, and finds out the rich city is stealing his town's water. Then it turns into a thing about patents and voting. The robot's good, and there's a really good part with Ada and her mom."

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- **Issue 01:** Strong hook and a robot I liked, but I didn't know what Alpha was or what Alex wanted until page 15, and the cliffhanger about Tomas contradicted itself.
- **Issue 02:** A fetch quest through four strangers' labs that felt like an economics assignment, saved a little by Lock, Jalen and the connector fix, and it forgot about Tomas.
- **Issue 03:** The Ada and Leona scene and "Pipe says eighteen" are the best things in the book, but the world finally gets explained on page 41, the climax is screens, and I never found out what happened to the dad.


# cold-read-b.md (from the room)

# Cold Read B — Prosperity

Read cold, all 54 pages, three 18-page issues, the night before it was due. I did not choose this book. Page counts check out: Issue 01 is pages 1–18, Issue 02 is 19–36, Issue 03 is 37–54. Everything below is what happened to me while reading, not what I worked out afterwards.

---

## Issue 01 — Keel (pages 1–18)

### Pulled me forward
- Page 1: the unapproved-repair exchange. "That isn't the approved repair." / "Then don't approve it." I was expecting a lecture and got a kid with a scarred hand on a pump. Fine, I'm looking.
- Page 2: the birthday debt screen is the best thing in the issue. 418,607 credits, 28.7 years, "Happy birthday, Phantum." I read every line of that screen. That's a real gut-punch and it costs the page nothing.
- Page 13: "The survey says straight. The bolts say left." Concrete, visual, I understood it instantly. This is the book at its best — physical truth versus official record, no speech.
- Page 14–15: the cold pipe and the vibrating pipe, then REPORTED 62% / DELIVERED 18%. I got genuinely angry at that number. That's the hook of the whole book and it works because nobody explains it, they just show two pipes.
- TJ's pieces wriggling across the floor while his head watches the foreman (page 11). Most fun I had in the issue.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Page 8: a woman seen from behind clicks TRACK instead of REPORT TO ALPHA. I get that it's meant to be ominous but I don't know who she is, so I watched it happen and felt nothing.
- Pages 15–16: the Measure is sitting in a fitted recess exactly where it's needed, does exactly the three things the plot needs. I muttered "convenient" and kept going.

### I was confused
- Page 9: "I missed the first installment." Ada said "same amount next week" on page 3, and everything since reads like a day or two. When did a week pass?
- Page 9: Ada suddenly knows the secret pipe-mark system ("every third junction has a pipe mark"). How does the medicine lender know the abandoned mine better than the map?
- Page 16: the choice is spelled out as binary — slip out the side passage, or send the evidence and "go back through Tomas's door" (i.e., get caught). He sends it. Then page 17 he's at an ascent entrance and Mera's opened a third route. The stated price of sending just evaporates. I reread pages 16–17 twice to see what I missed. I don't think I missed anything; the consequence got cheated.
- Pages 17–18: who opened what, and why does the "rescue" route fill with water while they're inside it? Miners open a residential regulator, Mera opens a conduit segment, the conduit floods around the heroes. I couldn't tell if the water was helping Keel, attacking them, or just happening. Geography of the climax is mud.
- Page 18: "TOMAS — SIGNAL LOST." I just saw Tomas alive and limping two panels earlier (page 17), at Site 6, with the miners. He was never in the conduit, so "No Tomas is visible" in the cliffhanger panel means nothing, and since when does Alex's wage-band track a coworker's life signal? Read as manufactured stakes. I didn't buy it.

### Things I was expected to already know
- Alpha. Page 5, "pre-Alpha pipes"; page 8, "[REPORT TO ALPHA]." Never explained anywhere in the issue. A company? A government? An era? I guessed "the system that runs everything" and read on, but I was being asked to feel unease about a word.
- The Measure (page 14). Capital-M device, hidden in the wall, three perfect functions. Nobody says who made it or why it's there.
- TJ's name. Page 10's description just starts calling the assembled dog "TJ." Nobody names him on-panel. Minor, but I noticed the name arrive from nowhere.
- Mera (page 8). A name and the back of a head.
- Grandmother's hand-bound book with the water-drop mark (page 4). It works as the shelf key, I think, but it's never opened and never comes back. What's in it?

### Lines I read twice
- "Leaving doesn't make you free if somebody else carries the cost" (page 3). Read it twice. It sounds wise, but I couldn't attach it to anyone specific — and by the end of the issue Alex leaves his sick, confused grandmother alone in Keel and nobody, including the book, says a word about who carries that cost. The line accuses and then the story does the thing.
- "Somewhere the records forgot" (page 7). Cute, vague, read twice, moved on.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Alex, Ada, B11, Tomas, Grandmother — all distinct. B11's dry voice ("Thinking about it isn't doing it") is the best voice in the issue. The guard, the bouncer and Foreman-7 blur into one uniform, but they're one-scene men so it doesn't cost much. Mera is a silhouette with a name tag.

### I felt something
- Page 2: the debt transfer. Anger on his behalf.
- Page 10: he steps over the yellow line and loses the 40 credits he earned today — the same 40 from the birthday screen. Felt that.
- Page 15: the 18%. Real anger at a fictional number.

### I predicted
- The dad's secret room (called it at "He's closer than you think," page 4).
- The rich city is taking the water — I called it at page 14's two pipes, before the 18% confirmed it.
- Alex would send the evidence rather than slip away. The book's moral shape is visible from page 1.
- Tomas's "signal lost" is a fake-out. (Page 52 proves me right.)

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A debt-trapped kid finds physical proof that the city's water records are lies, and the problem is whether proof can do anything.

### Where I would have put it down
Nowhere in this issue. It moves, the hook is clean, and the 62/18 reveal landed. The flooding-conduit muddle on pages 17–18 is where I shrugged, not where I stopped.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 18: climbing toward the light with water rising below. That's a real cliffhanger — people I know, in danger I can see — even though the Tomas "signal lost" beat misfired because I'd just watched him limp around alive. Yes, I'd turn to Issue 02. Mostly I want to know what the 18% proof does to the people upstairs, and whether Adrian is dead.

VERDICT Issue 01: put down: none; next issue: yes

---

## Issue 02 — Halyard (pages 19–36)

### Pulled me forward
- Page 21: Lock. "Rights under dispute are not a wallet" — and especially "Protected from what?" / "From being asked to choose while frightened." That's a properly chilling villain line. He's calm, he's reasonable, and he wants everything.
- Page 25: B11 counting bodies. "Five people. Two machines. The patrol will classify six active bodies." / "TJ's a dog." / "The system has not met him." I actually laughed. Best beat in the issue.
- Page 28: the salvaged-sleeve fix — filing an edge so two parts that were never allowed to connect can connect — is a good quiet callback to page 1's unapproved repair. I noticed it and it worked on me.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 23–26: four pages, four collaborators, same scene four times. Arrive, receive part, thematic line, security door closes. By Suri's page (24) I'd spotted the pattern; by Jalen's (25) I was skimming. Ren's page (26) I barely read.
- Pages 31–32: the rebuild montage is four people announcing their sub-problem in turn ("The membrane needs area." / "The filter needs rest." / "The power can cycle." / "The heat can feed the filter."). It reads like a worksheet. Skimmed.
- Page 30: the big theme speech. B11: "I counted the record and missed the people. That was my error. What would you do?" The robot confesses the moral of the book and then hands moral authority to a seventeen-year-old. I didn't slow down because I was lost; I slowed down because I was being lectured, and I can smell a lesson.

### I was confused
- Page 22: Alex rattles off "Lina. Suri. Jalen. Ren." — four names never mentioned before, by a kid who has never met them, before any scene shows him learning them. I flipped back thinking I'd skipped a page. I hadn't.
- Page 27: Lina said "Adrian left each of us a piece" — Adrian's own pieces — and then Adrian's own pieces don't fit together? "Vector standard rejects the Caldera cycle." So were these rebuilt to House standards? If they're the original pieces, why don't they interface? The metaphor (systems built to lock) is clear; the logic isn't.
- Page 28 vs page 33: SIMULATED RECOVERY goes 94% and then later 91%, with nobody remarking on it. The number went down. Why? A math-nerd reader notices.
- Page 31: "The four collaborators return to the room." Suri walked out with the group, Jalen explicitly said he wasn't coming, Ren shoved a module through a closing door and stayed behind it. When did all four get past House security into the maker room?
- Page 35: "Earlier projected images were translucent; this object casts a solid shadow." What earlier projected images? There is no earlier appearance of this medallion in the pages I read. This reads like a callback to a scene that doesn't exist. Gave up on it.
- Page 36: "BOUNDED SUMMONS ISSUED." Summons to where, issued by what authority, and what does "bounded" limit? Also — where did Grandmother go? Alex has been in two cities for days and his demented grandmother is alone in Keel with, I assume, the medicine Ada sells. Nobody mentions her once in the whole issue. The book opened by telling me leaving dumps the cost on someone else.

### Things I was expected to already know
- Morrow & Sons (page 20). A fair Keel business on a screen, nobody we've met, shown like it matters. It matters on page 54; here it's a name.
- The Charter Compact (page 21). The thing Lock wants the estate signed to. Never defined.
- "The Houses were selected for scale" (page 20). Selected how, when, by whom? "That is what the record says" is not an answer, and the book knows it.
- Alpha, again (page 20 — first time anyone says the name aloud: "By Alpha?"). Twenty pages in and the reader still has no working definition.
- The Seal (page 35). A bronze medallion Lina has carried for fifteen years; it warms, a screen says CONTRIBUTION ATTRIBUTION REGISTERED. What it is, what system it registers to, why it matters — all deferred.
- Mera's "dark Covenant band" (page 36, description text). "Covenant" appears with zero context.
- "One deadline" (page 26). What deadline?

### Lines I read twice
- "From being asked to choose while frightened" (page 21). Twice, because it's good.
- "That's what he's selling" (page 22). Twice, because I had to unpack it — walking away is the product. Fine, got there.
- "I counted the record and missed the people" (page 30). Understood on first read; the problem isn't confusion, it's that the book stopped trusting me.
- Page 35's "earlier projected images" line. Read twice, gave up.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Lock: completely distinct, best character in the issue. The four collaborators: defined by their components, not their selves. Suri stuck ("someone who notices when it stops breathing" — good line). Jalen stuck only as "the one who wouldn't come." Ren was "welding person." By the page 31 montage I was flipping back to check who brought membrane. And Lina's surname is VEY (page 26), which is going to collide with VEYRA next issue — I can feel it coming.

### I felt something
- Page 21: "choose while frightened" — cold little shiver.
- Page 25: the TJ/bodies exchange — actual laugh.
- Page 30: what I felt was embarrassment, for the book.

### I predicted
- Alex refuses to sign. Obvious from the moment the offer is made.
- The five parts fail on first assembly. Genre rhythm, called it.
- Lock threatens the collaborators. Called it; he does it twice.
- Ada is more than a Keel medicine lender. Her page-9 pipe knowledge made me suspicious she's connected upstairs.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Now it's about who owns ideas — the Houses own everything their workers make, and Alex won't hand over his father's estate. (Note: this is a different book from Issue 01's water-theft story. Two issues, two subjects.)

### Where I would have put it down
Page 25. Third identical errand scene in a row, and I'd figured out there was a fourth coming. In a shop, that's where it goes back on the shelf.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 36 is a cursor selecting SUMMON from a menu. As a cliffhanger it's nothing — a bureaucratic click, no question I need answered, nobody I care about standing in it. What carries me into Issue 03 is the leftover business: Adrian's fate, what Mera even is, whether Lock burns the four collaborators. A tired yes, and it's no thanks to the last page itself.

VERDICT Issue 02: put down: page 25; next issue: yes

---

## Issue 03 — Oasis (pages 37–54)

### Pulled me forward
- Page 37: the gate hesitates for Alex and opens instantly for Ada — "VEYRA, A. — STATUS: UNRESOLVED." Now that's a hook. One screen recontextualized a whole character.
- Pages 39–40: Ada and Leona. "Did you know where I was?" / "Within a year." / "And you didn't come." I sat up. Then "You chose safety instead of me" and "Watching is not knowing." / "Then don't call it care." Best sustained scene in the book.
- Page 44: the three screens crushing Adrian — parts denied, travel restricted, pursuit pattern. "First, people stopped selling to him." / "Then people stopped standing near him." Three UI cards do more worldbuilding than forty pages of the word "Alpha." This is where Alpha finally became scary instead of a name.
- Page 45: Adrian's recording. "Alex. What you do with this is up to you." The cut before his death is right; the scene lands.
- Pages 48–49: the temptation. "Take executive authority… you could correct it tonight." And Ada: "That's still two people deciding for everyone else." / "Don't give me that much power." For one panel, when Alex said "We could share it," I genuinely wasn't sure which way he'd go. Best scene in the issue.
- Pages 52–53: "Paper says sixty-two." / "Pipe says eighteen." The numbers came back as characters. "The allocation is compliant." / "The water isn't." I grinned. That's the whole book in six words, and nobody speechifies it.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 50–51: the procedure pages. Evidence placed, statements read, and then the climax card: DESIGNATED STRUCTURE REGISTERED: DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL. I read it twice because I couldn't believe that was the finale. Page 51's victory screen is a five-item job description for Alpha. I get that the dryness is the point — the emotional climax already happened on page 48 — but my eyes still slid.
- Page 47: "THREE COMPONENTS DETECTED." The Measure, the Seal and the bands are suddenly a matched set of three keys, and I noticed the collect-three-artifacts skeleton only now, at the moment it's cashed. Each piece arrived by convenience (found in a recess, carried in a uniform, sitting in a robot's chest), so the assembly feels dealt, not earned.

### I was confused
- Page 41: Adrian's Covenant band is revealed inside B11's chest compartment, as if I knew it was there. Nobody planted it. (Also that chest now holds a membrane component, a brass band and the Measure. It's a clown car.)
- Page 41: "We built the Covenant during the Water War. Two of three custodians could authorize emergency authority." This is the actual premise of the entire world — what Alpha is, why it has power, why nobody can switch it off — and it arrives on page 41 of 54. I understood the whole book backwards from here. Everything before was me guessing.
- Mera. Three issues in: she has keys, an override panel, a band, a promise to Leona. What is her job? Who does she answer to? Never said. She's a function wearing a name.
- Grandmother. Never mentioned. Not once, in either city, by anyone. Sick, demented, alone, and the story that scolded "somebody else carries the cost" never pays her a thought. I kept waiting.
- Page 54: the debt drops from 418,607 to 402,110 — 16,497 credits — in "weeks," by a kid whose wage is 40 a day. That's over a year of full wages in weeks. Unless purifier money, which is never stated. The math doesn't work.
- Page 54: "Alex makes a payment to Ada… ADA VEYRA — PERSONAL BALANCE REDUCED." If he's repaying her, why does her balance go down? Read it three times. Either she's in debt too (never said) or the screen means his outstanding loan (then say that). Unresolved.
- Adrian's fate: WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED, a flashback that cuts before the death, Grandmother's "He's closer than you think" — and then nothing. Hook or dropped thread, I can't tell, and I felt the lack.

### Things I was expected to already know
- The Water War (page 41). The founding catastrophe, first named at page 41, spoken like common knowledge.
- The Covenant and its two-of-three rule (page 41). The book's actual rulebook, delivered in dialogue near the end.
- The "legacy node" (page 47). A socket that takes the three artifacts, appearing exactly when the plot needs one.
- Alpha. Final verdict on the ledger: name used from page 5, working definition assembled around pages 41–44. Forty pages of being asked to feel a word.

### Lines I read twice
- "I traded a few terrible days I could see for fifteen years I couldn't" (page 40). Twice; landed.
- "Alpha recorded 'later' as permission to continue" (page 41). Twice; the entire book in one line, thirteen pages from the end.
- "Her personal balance decreases" (page 54). Three times; still unsure.
- "DESIGNATED STRUCTURE REGISTERED: DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL" (page 50). Twice, in disbelief.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
Ada becomes the best person in the book this issue. Leona is distinct. And here it is: Lina VEY versus Leona VEYRA versus Ada VEYRA. On page 38 I genuinely thought Lina was about to be Ada's mother or aunt. Three near-identical surnames, no relationship between them, never addressed. The three civic workers (gauge worker, maintenance rep, allocation clerk) are walking job titles, but they're plainly meant to be, so it doesn't hurt.

### I felt something
- Page 39: "You chose safety instead of me." Felt it.
- Page 46: "He left you a choice." / "He was still a gambler." / "And he still built something worth finding." / "Also yes." Felt that too — the book letting Adrian be both things.
- Page 48: "Don't give me that much power." Best thing Ada does all book.
- Page 49: the refusal has a price — workshop sealed, clearance expiring, debt stays. I respected the book here. It didn't pay him off for being good.
- Page 53: "The water isn't." Grinned.
- Page 54: "You still thinking about leaving?" / "Every day." / "Good." Quiet, earned, worked.

### I predicted
- Mera is tied to Ada's past. Right.
- Alex refuses executive power. Right, though the "we could share it" feint briefly got me.
- The debt is not magically fixed. Right — and I was glad to be right; an erased debt would have made me put the book down on the last page out of spite.
- Adrian's death is shown or answered. Wrong — and I'm still a little annoyed about it.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
An emergency system never got switched off because the permission had no expiry date, and the answer is that nobody — not even a good kid — should get to hold the controls alone. (Third issue, third subject: water theft, then ownership, then governance.)

### Where I would have put it down
Page 50. The civic-hall procedure is where the book stops being a story and starts being a model of a process. By then I was too close to the end to actually quit, but that's where the reading became duty.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 54 is an overlook, an open appeal marker, and two people not deciding things for each other. It's a good ending for this book — and it closes the book. Nothing on it pulls me forward. The one thread that could (is Adrian alive?) was deliberately left to dangle, but the story just spent three issues teaching me not to expect adventure payoffs, so I don't expect one. If a next book exists, it's about an appeals process. I wish these people well and I would not buy it.

VERDICT Issue 03: put down: page 50; next issue: no

---

## Whole book

### The page that would have lost my whole class
Page 51. The climax of the book, the moment everything turns, and the big screen reads: "ALPHA ROLE: OPERATION / MONITORING / MAINTENANCE / ACCOUNTING / ALERTS." The payoff of 51 pages is a job description. Half the class is on their phones by MAINTENANCE. Page 50's "DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL" is the warm-up act that gets them reaching for their pockets.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
A kid inherits half a million credits of his missing dad's debt on his seventeenth birthday, finds out the rich cities upstairs are stealing his town's water and faking the numbers, and instead of blowing anything up he proves it with gauges, builds a home water filter with his dad's old work crew so no company can own it, gets offered emergency control of the whole system and turns it down, and the happy ending is a public complaint process that actually works. There's also a robot dog that comes apart into pieces and it's the best character. It's smarter than it sounds and slower than it should be, and it absolutely is a lesson, but the good bits — the lying gauges, the mum scene, "the water isn't" — are good enough that I finished it without hating it.

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- Issue 01: Rust, debt and a number that lies — a kid proves the water's being stolen and I was genuinely in.
- Issue 02: Four strangers hand over four parts in the same scene four times while a polite man threatens everyone with paperwork, and the dog gets the only laugh.
- Issue 03: Mum left, dad's tape plays, the villain turns out to be a permission slip nobody ever cancelled, and the ending is a committee I'm glad exists and never want to read about again.

# Prosperity: Analysis (Issues 01–03, pages 1–54)

I read the pages only, the way each person below would meet them.

---

## The political read

| Reading | Signal | Pages that carry it |
|---|---|---|
| **Progressive** | **Strong (on the surface)** | p2: a 17-year-old inherits 418,607 credits of household liability on his birthday. p14–15: water is quietly diverted from the poor residential line to industry ("REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%"), which reads like Flint. p20: a young worker's invention becomes Vector House property for a "CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS." p26, p29: a corporate director threatens the workers who helped. p52–53: a community challenge to a "compliant" allocation. |
| **Libertarian** | **Some to strong (underneath)** | p41: emergency authority with "no expiration. No independent revocation. We thought we could take it back later." p44: Adrian is debanked and cut off before he is chased ("First, people stopped selling to him"). p8, p40: surveillance passed off as care ("Watching is not knowing"). p20: the Houses "were selected for scale. By Alpha?", which is cronyism, not a market. p48–49: the hero turns down total power. p51: debts and agreements stay "UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS." |
| **Conservative** | **Some** | Keeping your word on a debt (p3, p9, p54). Duty to family (Grandmother, p4). Owning your choices: Leona says "Both choices were mine" (p42). Gambling shown as a vice that hurt other people (p2, "For everybody else"). No handouts. Faith, tradition and community institutions are absent. |
| **Socialist** | **Some** | p27, p31: production by a collective, with five contributors around one machine. p33: "PATENT STATUS: UNFILED," "No exclusive owner." p54: "ALLOCATION REVIEW: COMMUNITY-PENDING." Water is handed out by a public table, never priced. |
| **Capitalist, bad way** | **Strong** | Caldera, Vector and Orbital Houses (p19–36). Cassian Lock's offer: debt cleared if Alex signs over the estate, and the collaborators named if he refuses (p21–22, p29). The kiosk (p20). "HOUSE PRODUCTION AUTHORIZED / CONTRIBUTOR ACCESS REVIEW PENDING" (p36). |
| **Capitalist, good way** | **Weak to some** | Ada's honest loan: "Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees" (p3). Morrow & Sons, which posts its price, wage and margin (p20, p54). Alex in paid service work (p54). These add up to about three panels of positive enterprise against seventeen pages of the Houses. |

**What the surface invites:** an anti-corporate dystopia, where the rich up the mountain steal water from the poor below and big companies own your work. A teenager flipping through Issue 02 will read it that way.

**What the story supports:** a more libertarian and personal-responsibility book. The Houses are creatures of Alpha, a state system that picked them. The real villain is emergency power nobody took back (p41) and a record trusted over the physical world (p52: "Paper says sixty-two. / Pipe says eighteen."). The hero refuses a buyout (p34) and refuses absolute power (p49), and he keeps paying (p54). No debt is forgiven.

**Who stops reading because of the surface:** a business-owning parent or a centre-right teacher who skims pp. 20–29. They see a corporation buying a dead man's patents, threatening workers, and a hero who answers "No exclusive owner" (p33). The line that tells them the Houses were state-picked (p20) is hedged ("That is what the record says"), so they don't catch it. A Reynolds-minded reader is most at risk of quitting in Issue 02 and never reaching the payoffs on pp. 41–51. At the other end, a progressive student may finish annoyed that the hero calmly keeps paying an imposed debt (p54). That reader keeps going but argues with it, which is not a complaint.

## Young Americans Center

**What they would like**
- **Ada's loan is a clean, accurate model of personal credit.** Medicine first, terms stated, "Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees" (p3).
- **Alex owns a missed payment.** He misses the first installment and tells her before she asks ("Then tell me before I have to ask." / "I'm telling you." p9).
- **The book ends on repayment, not rescue.** Fourteen months later he is still paying: "LOAN BALANCE REDUCED," "Same amount next week" (p54). That is exactly the Daniels story: keeping your word after it gets hard.
- **No one cancels the debt.** It goes from 418,607 to 402,110 (p2 → p54), and the numbers add up: 40 credits a day for about 14 months. Alex turns down the buyout that would have cleared it (p21–22, p34). He also turns down the executive power that would have erased it (p48–49). The system leaves debts "UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS" (p51). This is the opposite of "someone powerful cancels it," and YAC will notice.
- **He takes initiative.** The improvised repair on p1: "Then don't approve it. … Just notice it works."
- **Integrity costs him something.** He gives up a day's wage to save Tomas (p10), and his refusal "has a price" (p49).
- **Morrow & Sons is a business that serves people and makes money.** It posts price, wage and margin (p20, p54).

**What would bother them**
- The p2 debt mechanics. A minor automatically takes on a parent's liability, and a teenager can't reliably tell a dystopia rule from how credit works. They are a real bank, and this is the item they are most likely to raise.
- The only line about banks is a dig (p3).
- Issue 02 casts large firms as villains for seventeen pages. Morrow & Sons gets two panels, and the "FAIR PRICE" label (p20) reads like a moral stamp, not a price.
- The climax is a civic hearing, not an enterprise. Pages 47–53 are governance. The free-enterprise moments are crowded into p54, panel 1.
- After "No exclusive owner" (p33) the book never shows who gets paid for the purifier. A YouthBiz coach will ask what the business model is.
- Partisan cues are roughly balanced: the water-justice signal leans left, the emergency-power signal leans right. That suits "carefully nonpartisan" better than most books manage.

**Likely verdict: partly.** They would be glad to hand Ada's loan and p54 to a classroom. They would want the p2 inheritance mechanics and the p3 bank line handled before it reaches a Denver public school. They would wish the enterprise were the story rather than the epilogue.

---

## Bill Reynolds

**What he would like**
- **No windfall solves the plot.** Lock's deal is a textbook bailout: "Your debt clears tonight" (p21). Alex refuses it twice (p22: "That's what he's selling"; p34: "No."). He also refuses unlimited power (p49), and he is still paying at the end. That is "There is No Free Lunch" in plot form.
- **The beer-hall story is here in miniature.** He misses a payment, faces the lender, and keeps paying (p9, p54).
- **The mentor is wrong, admits it, and then asks.** B11 blames the membrane chemistry and is wrong (p28). His risk table counts only the record (p30). He then says "I counted the record and missed the people. That was my error. What would you do?" (p30). That is very close to "How do you see it? What are we missing?"
- **Technology cannot replace presence.** Alpha's whole failure is trusting the record over people and pipes. Pages 47 and 51 require humans in the process ("HUMAN ROLE REQUIRED"). B11 never replaces Ada, Tomas or the collaborators.
- **Government overreach and cronyism are the deeper villains.** The emergency power nobody took back (p41), the debanking (p44), and Houses "selected" by Alpha (p20). The word "capitalism" never appears.
- **The failure is quick.** 11% to 94% to a modest 91% household unit that still needs maintenance (p27–33).

**What would bother him**
- **Business owners look like villains by default** unless you catch the half-line on p20. Lock is the face of business in this book.
- **De Soto runs the wrong way.** Adrian's 312 patents are literally dead capital: "Rights under dispute are not a wallet" (p21). The book leaves them dead. "No exclusive owner" (p33) is celebrated, and the attribution record (p35) records credit, not property anyone can use. "Ownership ends a surprising number of arguments" is the moral he'd want; here it is a committee that ends the argument (p50–53).
- **Alex never fails big.** He is right almost every time: the repair, the bolts, the connectors, the refusals. His one failure is a missed installment. Reynolds' best project was a failure that taught him the most, and Alex never gets one.
- **The dog** is called TJ, and the page never says it is for a Founder (p11). He might enjoy the nod if he guesses it.
- **There is one lecture line**, B11's "One business earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale." (p20)

**Does Bi11bot sound like him? No.** The profile asks for plain, slow, slightly roundabout Western speech: a question first, then a story from his own life, then one plain line, with jokes at his own expense. B11 speaks in short, dry, precise machine lines: "Correct." (p16, twice); "A versatile word." (p13); "Trace shows where. Not why." (p15); "That is generally what connectors are for." (p27). He tells no stories. He never mentions a failure of his own until p30, and even that is a correction, not a story. There is no "damn hard." The closest he comes to self-deprecating humour is "I expected a longer failure" (p28). He asks a real question exactly once (p30). Also, the book calls him **B11**, never Bi11bot. Structurally he is right: he doesn't hand out answers, he is sometimes wrong, he steps back. The voice is not Reynolds'.

**Likely verdict: partly. Close to yes on substance, short on voice and on business.** He would not finish feeling the book argues against him. Its plot is more aligned with him than its surface. But he would not hear himself in his own robot, and he would wince at Issue 02.

---

## A comic writer

**The hook:** strong. Page 1 delivers a competent kid, an unapproved fix and a dare of a line. Page 2 gives you a birthday that comes with "PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS" plus "My debt face." A pro keeps reading past page ten.

**Page turns:** mixed. The B11 reveal falls correctly on a left page after a turn (p6). But pp. 4–5 are a spread, so the bookshelf's "CLICK—RUMBLE" and the open workshop are seen together: the reveal is spoiled. Issue endings on p18 and p36 are well placed.

**A cliffhanger that undoes itself.** Page 18 ends on "TOMAS SITE 6 — SIGNAL LOST … The question is not answered." But p17, panel 2 has already shown "Tomas … alive and limping." A writer would circle this first.

**Clarity problems a pro would flag:**
- The p17–18 valve business is unclear. Is Mera rescuing them or drowning them? The script works hard to say the residential regulator is "elsewhere on the diagram," and no reader will see that.
- Page 54 calls panel 4 a "FULL-PAGE FINAL IMAGE," which is impossible on a four-panel page. It would need its own page, and the count is fixed at 54.

**Dialogue:** the first issue is sharp ("You look expensive." / "It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty."). By Issue 02, everyone (Lock, Lina, Ren, Mera, Leona, Ada) speaks in the same aphoristic register, and the four collaborators are one technical line each (pp. 23–26). Pages 47–51 are mostly screen text.

**Splash pages:** p1 earns it. p37 is a good arrival at Oasis, but it is cluttered with two insets.

**What they would cut or compress:**
- The fetch-quest rhythm of Issue 02 (one collaborator per page, pp. 23–26).
- The procedural screens on pp. 47–51.
- The quest for three objects (Measure, Seal, Covenant bands), which reads like a game design document.

**Would they take the job?** Yes, on Issue 01 and the p38–40 mother-daughter scene, which is the best writing in the book. They would ask to rebuild the back half of Issue 03 so the climax is something a person *does*, not a protocol that registers.

---

## A game designer

**There is a game here, and a good one.**
- **The loop:** shift work for 40 credits, a weekly fixed installment to Ada, choices that dock your pay, and checking the record against the physical gauge. It plays like *Papers, Please* crossed with *Frostpunk*, with a ledger always on screen (p2, p9, p54).
- **Choices that cost something, on the page:**
  - Step across the line and lose the wage (p10).
  - The one-use quiet exit versus the public broadcast (p16).
  - Sign the estate away (debt cleared, collaborators safe) or refuse (p22, p29).
  - Take executive power or keep your workshop and clearance (p48–49).

  The book says it outright: "Then the refusal has a price."
- **Systems players would push on:**
  - TJ's detachable body as a scouting and puzzle tool (p11, p13).
  - Connector-fitting by touch (p28).
  - Juggling the purifier's limits: area, rest cycles, heat recovery (p31–32).
  - Reputation with each House.
  - Whether to repay early or late, and what Ada does if you miss.
- **What's thin:** there is no economy beyond one wage and one loan. Morrow & Sons, a business the player could run, is the obvious missing mode. It also fits Young AmeriTowne neatly.

**Would they want to build it?** Yes. The record-versus-reality mechanic and the debt clock are a working core loop already.

---

## A streaming showrunner

**The engine:** a vertical class world in three tiers (Keel, Halyard, Oasis), a missing-father mystery, a debt clock and a water conspiracy. It is easy to pitch: *Snowpiercer* stood on end, with a debt instead of a train.

**Characters an audience follows for a season:**
- Alex. Competent, wry, not a chosen one.
- Ada. Her history with Leona carries real emotional weight (pp. 38–40).
- B11 and TJ. TJ, the dog that comes apart, sells merchandise.
- Mera. The most interesting adult: complicit, sorry, still controlling.
- Lock. A reasonable-sounding antagonist, which is good, but he has no life of his own.

**Season-one cliffhanger:** the flooding conduit (p18), or better, Adrian's fate. "The sequence cuts before Adrian's evacuation or death is shown" (p45), plus Grandmother's "He's closer than you think" (p4). That is a season-two engine, if the show keeps Grandmother, whom the book drops after p5.

**What's missing:**
- An antagonist with a face and wants. Alpha is abstract, and Lock leaves the board after p34.
- A climax that plays as action. Pages 47–53 are a hearing, and a showrunner would make it the mid-season turn, not the finale.
- Stakes for the four collaborators. Their fates are "ACCESS REVIEW PENDING" (p36), and we never see them lose anything.

**Verdict:** they would option it on Issue 01 and the Ada/Leona thread, then rebuild the finale.

---

## Does it smell like school

**Pages where something is explained so the reader can learn it, or a line states the lesson. Count: 10.**
1. **p3.** "Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees." It is in character, but it reads like a credit-union brochure.
2. **p20.** "FAIR PRICE / SERVICE INCLUDED" as a label, plus B11's "One business earns customers. The Houses were selected for scale." This is the textbook contrast stated outright.
3. **p26.** "Waste heat is still material. Vent it and you lose the system." A science-class line.
4. **p31.** "If a household can't clean it, it doesn't own it." The ownership moral, spoken outright.
5. **p42.** "I chose emergency authority. I chose distance from my daughter. Both choices were mine." A responsibility statement delivered *into a recording terminal*, almost to camera.
6. **p47.** "HUMAN ROLE REQUIRED: CONVENOR / AUTHENTICATOR," then "I convene it. I don't own it." A term being defined.
7. **p50.** "Physical flow. / Maintenance capacity. / Reserve continuity." and "DISTRIBUTED VERIFICATION PROTOCOL." Civics vocabulary.
8. **p51.** "RESCINDED WITHIN DEFINED SCOPE" / "UNCHANGED PENDING HUMAN PROCESS." The process explained in captions.
9. **p53.** "It's slow." / "It's visible." The theme stated as a closing couplet.
10. **p54, panel 1.** "A worker records cost, wage and margin." Unit-economics shown as a demonstration.

The school smell is concentrated in pp. 47–53. A teen reading the night before will hit this stretch last, and it is the part they will remember.

**Pages that teach without the smell, because people need the thing and pay for it:**
- **p1.** The working fix versus the approved one.
- **p2.** The debt clock does the arithmetic for you.
- **p9.** A missed installment, and the honesty that costs face.
- **p10.** −40 credits for saving a man.
- **pp. 14–15.** A hand on a cold pipe and a hand on a full one.
- **p22.** "That's what he's selling."
- **p28.** "The parts aren't wrong. The edges are."
- **p49.** "Then the refusal has a price."
- **p52.** "Paper says sixty-two. / Pipe says eighteen." The best teaching line in the book.
- **p54, panels 2–3.** The balance going down slowly, week after week.

The first issue mostly teaches by cost. The third mostly teaches by caption.

**Verdict: yes.** It smells of school in the back third. Issue 01 alone would be a no.

---

## What would change the verdicts

1. **p20 (YAC, Reynolds).** Turn B11's explaining line into a short scene where the reader *sees* Alpha awarding a House its charter or its water. That way the Houses read as state-picked cronies, not as what markets produce, before the skimming parent quits.
2. **pp. 32–33 or p54 (Reynolds, YAC).** Give Alex a real failure he owns. One possibility: the first Morrow & Sons units fail in Keel homes, and he has to face the customers and Ada about the parts he bought on credit. Then he pays it down. Right now his only failure is one missed installment.
3. **p54 (Reynolds, YAC).** Show the recorded attribution *earning*: the five contributors receive a share from each Morrow & Sons sale. That turns "No exclusive owner" (p33) into written-down, defensible property that becomes capital, and it answers the YouthBiz question of who gets paid.
4. **p30 or p46 (Reynolds).** Give B11 one scene in the profile's voice: a question, then a remembered failure of his own with Adrian shown in flashback panels, then one plain line, with the joke at his own expense. That would make the robot sound like the man who paid for the book.
5. **pp. 2 and 17–18 (YAC, the teen reader).** On p2, make clear on the page that the inherited liability is a rule of Keel imposed by Alpha, not how a loan works, so a teenager can tell it apart from Ada's honest loan. On p17, take Tomas out of panel 2 so the p18 cliffhanger holds, and make Mera's valve read as either rescue or threat at first glance.

---

## In short

Both partners are satisfied in part. YAC would gladly put Ada's loan and the repayment on p54 in front of a class. They would want the inherited debt on p2 and the bank line on p3 handled first, and they'd wish the business were the story, not the epilogue. Reynolds would get most of what he believes from the plot: no bailout, a mentor who is wrong and then asks, a debt still being paid. He would not hear himself in B11, and Issue 02 makes business look like the villain. The first issue teaches through what things cost; the last seven pages teach through captions.

VERDICT Young Americans Center: partly; Bill Reynolds: partly; smells like school: yes
